questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was an obligatory stay, arranged in connection to my study.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was an overall good experience, but it might be challenging to go to KNU, if you're going alone.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
Some of it was out a little late. For example, we got the wrong dorm address, and the correct one was only updated on the day of our arrival on a platform we weren't familiar with.
But the staff was super helpful and quick to reply. 
Orientation was adequate, but done on zoom along with the 'full time exchange students' and graduate students, so it was a little complicated to figure out what info was relevant to us, specifically.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
About a week before semester-start, we had an online zoom orientation. 
Upon arrival, there were people who helped check us in at the dorm and provided bedsheets. 
A couple of days after we had a physical welcome orientation. 
(Before arriving, our buddies helped with course selection and such, but this was a rather complicated issue).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
A dormitory. 
The housing isn't the best, as there are no fridges, and one shared microwave for the entire dormitory. 
So if you have special dietary restrictions, beware of food storage challenges. 
The rooms didn't seem to have been properly cleaned before we moved in, as there was leftover trash and stuff not cleaned properly off the walls when we arrived.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
There was a water automat for hot and cold water on each floor, and a shared microwave for the entire dorm. 
That is it.
There are convenience stores close to the dorms, and cafeterias around the school, but none close to the dorm.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Just the lack of cleanliness when moving in, and the lack of cooking facilities. 
The rooms are rather small but adequate. There is space to store everything and for your luggage trunks. There is a laundromat in the basement, and a very small gym. 
There is a small space between the room and windows to dry your laundry.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As mentioned, beware of your food options, if you have special dietary restrictions.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
We were not given the best information of this topic. 
Some of us, had help from our buddies, but they seemed just as confused. 
There were different signup dates for the different departments, and the exchange students get priority, but the days were spread out differently than explained. 
Furthermore, just because you can sign up for any course, doesn't mean that you should. 
Even though the classes are level 1 (so the start course), they may  not be catered towards beginners, so you should have som experience if you choose to take courses meant for certain majors.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Were were told certain dates that we, as exchange students, could sign up on. 
The course registration starts at noon Korean time, so at 3am here. As some of them fill up quickly, it would be advised to try so sign up then, or get your buddy to help you. 
The English courses couldn't be added on the pre-date (which we hadn't been informed of), but could only be accessed when the general registration period started. 
Then you signed up to your courses, and the first week of classes is a trial week, so after trying the classes, you could change them or drop them if they weren't for you.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The buddies can help a bit, but it differed how much, from buddy to buddy. They are responsible for helping you, but not doing the sign-up for you.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was rather lucky in getting all the courses i wanted, thanks to my buddy and being prepared with course numbers for signup.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Be prepared with all of your papers and course id's etc. for registration. 
The people at the uni are helpful, but a bit unclear at times. 
But contact them if you have issues. They really would love to help, and do their best to accommodate you.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Some of the English courses were very low-level, and I don't think I learned all that much from them. 
And some of the Korean courses didn't adhere to the curriculum and syllabus, so the course was completely different from its desription (only relevant for Korean studies majors on obligatory stay).

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Some were very interesting and proper for uni level, but others left a bit to be desired in the academic aspects. 
The professors are super nice though, and as long as you show up to classes, you will do fine.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The Korean courses were a bit more strict and structured. There was marginally more oral presentations and more challenging written exams, but the courses in themselves were very informative. 
The English courses differed a lot. Some of them were very similar to the teaching style at KU, and others felt like a highschool course. 
The structure is very similar to that of college in the US.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Everyday Korean for foreigners. 
Pilates. 
Community service at an eveningschool for children age 5-8 (teaching english). 
Philosophy in the age of AI. 
Case Study of Corporate Management in Korea and Overseas.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
For Korean Studies Majors, I would recommend the 'Everyday Korean for foreigners' course. The course description doesn't fit, but you will learn a lot about academic Korean, how to do presentations, and write assignments. It is a challenging course, but the teacher is very good at meeting people at their level and trying to make it educational for everyone. 

I personally also gained a lot from partaking in Community Service. This was a great way to practice my Korean while getting to experience being in a Korean workplace. The staff don't speak English very good but are very welcoming and appreciative. 
And the kids are adorable and fun to teach. 

For the English courses, I would recommend any course with Professor Jay Park. She is very sharp and an incredibly passionate (and compassionate) teacher.

questions.answer:
Dorm fees were lower. 
Insurance was higher. 
Transportation was lower.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
There was a language exchange club, but they were not the most welcoming. 
And a lot of the clubs require you to be fluent in Korean to join, or are not available if you're only staying for a year.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Clubs. 
University festivals and events for exchange students.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The festivals. 
Join a club, if possible. It is hard to get local friends, otherwise.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Try do do social things. 
Go exploring. 
The nature in Chuncheon is incredible. 
Go hiking. 
Explore Korea. 
Go to the bars at humun. That's how you can socialize with the locals.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I already lived in South Korea for half a year before, so it wasn't personally a big issue.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join clubs and go to bars.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The caution when speaking with foreigners and using english.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness and kindness. If you just try to use a little korean, they are so happy.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Try to learn a bit of the language before you go. It is a bit far out, so not a lot of people know and are comfortable speaking English. 
Make sure to chick all the rules for dorm and required documents for your stay. 
Remember to have fun. School is of course important, but you would miss out on a really big part of your stay if you didn't engage in social activities etc. Culture is an equally big part of the stay.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Beware of your absence. You are only allowed to miss the classes per course before you automatically fail. 
But other than that, failing is nearly impossible.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The language and culture experience and the community service. By going a bit away from the main city, you truly get to experience the colours of Korea authentically.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Making local friends. They are not too eager to speak english sadly.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
